source: Parento editorial knowledge base, summarised from public guidance by WHO, AAP, IAP and CDC. General information only, not medical advice.

entries.answer:
- In a baby **under 3 months**, a temperature of **38°C (100.4°F) or higher** needs a doctor **right away**, even if the baby seems fine.
- Do not give fever medicine to a young infant unless a doctor tells you to.
- Keep feeding and dress the baby in light clothing while you get care.

- A fever is usually a sign the body is fighting an infection. How the child **acts** matters more than the exact number.
- Offer plenty of fluids, keep clothing light and let the child rest.
- Ask your doctor or pharmacist about the right fever medicine and dose for your child's **weight**.
- See a doctor if the fever lasts **more than 2-3 days**, goes above **40°C (104°F)**, or comes with a rash, stiff neck, trouble breathing, unusual sleepiness, or signs of dehydration.

- Watch for **fewer wet diapers** (fewer than 4 in 24 hours for a baby), dark urine, a dry mouth, no tears when crying, a sunken soft spot, or unusual sleepiness.
- Keep offering breast milk or formula; older children can take small, frequent sips of **ORS** (oral rehydration solution).
- Get medical help quickly if the child is very drowsy, has had no urine for 8 hours or more, or cannot keep fluids down.

- The main risk is **dehydration**, so give **ORS** in small, frequent sips and continue breastfeeding or normal feeds.
- In India, doctors commonly add **zinc** for 10-14 days for diarrhoea; ask your pediatrician for the right dose.
- Avoid fruit juices and sugary drinks, which can make diarrhoea worse.
- See a doctor for blood in the stool, repeated vomiting, a high fever, signs of dehydration, or diarrhoea lasting more than a few days.

- Hard, dry or painful stools are more important than how often the child goes.
- For children on solids, offer water, fruits like pear, papaya and prunes, vegetables and whole grains.
- Encourage active play and a relaxed potty routine after meals.
- See a doctor if there is blood, a swollen tummy, vomiting, or constipation in a young baby who is not yet on solids.

- Most colds get better on their own in 7-10 days.
- Saline nose drops and gentle suction help blocked noses, especially before feeds and sleep.
- **Do not give honey to babies under 12 months**, and avoid over-the-counter cough and cold medicines for young children unless a doctor advises them.
- Get help quickly for fast or noisy breathing, the skin pulling in between the ribs, bluish lips, or a baby who is too breathless to feed.

- **Trouble breathing, bluish lips or face, choking, or gasping is an emergency.** Call emergency services (112 in India) or go to the nearest hospital immediately.
- If the child is choking and cannot cry, cough or breathe, start infant or child choking first aid if you are trained, and call for help.

- Start solids at **around 6 months**, when the baby can sit with support, has good head control and shows interest in food.
- Begin with smooth or mashed foods such as rice-dal khichdi, mashed banana, or vegetable purées, then slowly increase texture and variety.
- Introduce **iron-rich foods** early (dal, egg yolk, meat, fortified cereals, green leafy vegetables).
- Continue breastfeeding alongside solids. Avoid added salt, sugar and honey in the first year.

- WHO recommends **exclusive breastfeeding for the first 6 months**, then continuing breastfeeding along with solid foods up to 2 years or beyond.
- Newborns usually feed **8-12 times in 24 hours**. Feed on demand.
- Signs the baby is getting enough include 6 or more wet diapers a day after the first week and steady weight gain.
- Pain while feeding often means a latch problem, so a lactation consultant or your pediatrician can help.

- Toddler appetite naturally goes up and down, and growth slows after the first year, so they often eat less than parents expect.
- Offer 3 meals and 2 snacks at regular times, and let the child decide how much to eat.
- Offer a new food many times (10-15 tries) without pressure.
- The best check is a **steady growth curve**. Talk to a doctor if the child is losing weight, has low energy, or is crossing down growth lines.

- Avoid cow's milk as a **main drink before 12 months**; breast milk or formula is best in the first year.
- From 6 months, small sips of water with meals are fine.
- After 12 months, around **2 cups (about 400-500 ml) of milk a day** is usually enough; too much milk can reduce appetite and contribute to iron deficiency.
- Fruit juice is not needed. Whole fruit is better.

- Common allergy foods such as egg and peanut (as smooth paste, **never whole nuts**) can usually be introduced from around 6 months, one at a time.
- If your child already has severe eczema or a known allergy, talk to your doctor before introducing these foods.
- **Swelling of the lips or face, trouble breathing, or repeated vomiting after a food is an emergency.** Seek care immediately.
- If a known allergy is recorded in Parento, always avoid that food unless your doctor advises otherwise.

- For children under 4-5 years, avoid **whole nuts, whole grapes, popcorn, hard candies and chunks of raw carrot or apple**.
- Cut round foods like grapes and cherry tomatoes into quarters lengthwise.
- Always supervise meals and keep the child seated while eating.

- Typical sleep needs: newborns 14-17 hours, 4-12 months 12-16 hours (with naps), 1-2 years 11-14 hours, 3-5 years 10-13 hours.
- A calm, predictable bedtime routine (bath, feed, book, song) helps.
- Night waking and 'sleep regressions' around 4, 8-10 and 18 months are common and usually pass in a few weeks.
- Talk to a doctor about loud snoring with pauses in breathing or extreme daytime sleepiness.

- Always place babies **on their back** to sleep, on a firm, flat surface.
- Keep pillows, quilts, soft toys and bumpers out of the sleep space.
- Room-sharing (baby in their own cot near your bed) is recommended for the first 6 months.
- Avoid overheating and keep the baby's environment smoke-free.

- First teeth usually appear between **6 and 12 months**.
- Drooling, chewing and mild fussiness are common. Teething does **not** cause high fever or diarrhoea; see a doctor if those happen.
- A clean, chilled (not frozen) teething ring or gently rubbing the gums with a clean finger can help.
- Avoid teething gels containing benzocaine and amber teething necklaces.

- Colic means a healthy baby crying for more than 3 hours a day, often in the evening. It usually peaks around 6 weeks and improves by 3-4 months.
- Try holding, gentle rocking, white noise, swaddling (for young babies) and burping during feeds.
- **Never shake a baby.** If you feel overwhelmed, put the baby safely in the cot and take a short break.
- See a doctor if crying comes with fever, vomiting, poor feeding, or a high-pitched cry.

- Change diapers often, clean gently with water, and let the skin air-dry.
- A thick layer of zinc oxide or petroleum jelly barrier cream protects the skin.
- See a doctor if the rash has blisters or pus, spreads, or does not improve in 2-3 days (it may be a yeast infection).

- Mild yellowing in the first week is common.
- See a doctor **promptly** if jaundice appears in the first 24 hours, spreads to the legs or palms, lasts beyond 2 weeks, or the baby is very sleepy or feeding poorly.
- Pale or chalky stools with dark urine need urgent review.

- Talk, sing and read with your child every day, and name objects and actions as you go.
- Respond to babbling and gestures as if it's a conversation, and pause to give them a turn.
- Limit screen time, which reduces back-and-forth talk.
- Talk to your doctor about a hearing check and speech assessment if there's no babbling by 9 months, no words by 16 months, or no two-word phrases by 24 months.

- Daily **tummy time** from the first weeks builds neck, back and arm strength.
- Give safe floor space to roll, crawl and pull up. Baby walkers are not recommended because they cause injuries and do not speed up walking.
- Most children walk independently between 9 and 18 months.
- See a doctor if the child is not sitting by 9 months, not walking by 18 months, or loses skills.

- Peek-a-boo, hiding toys under a cloth, stacking cups, shape sorters and simple puzzles build problem-solving.
- Read picture books daily and talk about what you see.
- Pretend play (cooking, doctor sets, dolls) builds imagination and language.
- Follow your child's interests; short, frequent play sessions work better than long ones.

- WHO and AAP advise **avoiding screens before 18-24 months**, except video calls with family.
- For **2-5 years**, limit screen time to **about 1 hour a day** of good-quality content, watched together when possible.
- Keep screens off during meals and for at least an hour before bed.

- Tantrums are normal between 1 and 4 years, while children are learning to handle big feelings.
- Stay calm, keep the child safe, and name the feeling ('You're upset because...').
- Praise good behaviour specifically, and keep routines predictable.
- Avoid hitting or shouting. Talk to a doctor if tantrums are very frequent, very long, or the child hurts themselves.

- Most children are ready between **18 months and 3 years**. Signs include staying dry for 2 hours, showing discomfort with a dirty diaper, and following simple instructions.
- Use a potty at regular times (after meals, before bath) and praise attempts.
- Expect accidents and never punish them.
- Night-time dryness often comes later, and bedwetting is common up to 5-6 years.

- Mild fever, fussiness, and redness or swelling at the injection site for 1-2 days are common.
- Keep feeding normally, cuddle and comfort the child, and ask your doctor about fever medicine.
- Seek care urgently for difficulty breathing, swelling of the face or lips, a seizure, crying for more than 3 hours, or unusual drowsiness.

- A missed vaccine usually **does not need to be restarted**. Your pediatrician can give a **catch-up schedule**.
- Book an appointment soon, since delays leave the child unprotected for longer.
- Bring the vaccination card so the doctor can see what has already been given.

- **Go to a hospital immediately** for trouble breathing, bluish lips, a seizure, unresponsiveness, severe dehydration, a non-blanching rash (spots that don't fade when pressed), or any fever in a baby under 3 months.
- **See a doctor the same day** for a fever lasting more than 2-3 days, ear pain, repeated vomiting, or a child who is unusually drowsy or irritable.
- Trust your instincts. If you feel something is wrong, get the child checked.

- Young children commonly get **6-10 colds a year**, especially after starting daycare.
- Other common illnesses are ear infections, viral stomach bugs, hand-foot-and-mouth disease, and viral rashes.
- Good handwashing, up-to-date vaccines, and breastfeeding (for infants) all reduce infections.
- Watch hydration, breathing and alertness, and see a doctor if any of these are affected.

- Iron needs rise from about 6 months, so offer iron-rich foods daily (dal, eggs, meat, ragi, green leafy vegetables) with vitamin C foods to help absorption.
- Many pediatricians recommend **vitamin D drops** for breastfed infants. Ask your doctor about the right dose for your child.
- Don't start supplements without medical advice, since too much iron can be harmful.

- Growth is best judged by the **trend over time** on a growth chart, not one number.
- Most babies double their birth weight by about 5 months and triple it by 12 months.
- Talk to your doctor if your child's measurements fall below the 3rd or above the 97th percentile, or cross two major percentile lines.

- **Seek emergency care** after a head injury if the child loses consciousness, vomits more than once, has a seizure, is unusually sleepy or confused, or has clear fluid or blood from the nose or ears.
- For babies under 1 year, any significant fall should be checked by a doctor.
- For minor bumps, apply a cold compress and watch the child closely for 24 hours.

- **This is an emergency.** Go to the nearest hospital or call emergency services (112 in India) immediately.
- Swallowed **button batteries or magnets** can cause serious internal injury within hours, even if the child seems fine.
- Do not make the child vomit. Take the container or packet with you.

- **During a seizure:** lay the child on their side on a safe surface, do not put anything in their mouth, and note the time.
- **Call emergency services (112) if it lasts more than 5 minutes**, if breathing is difficult, or if it's the first seizure.
- Every first seizure needs a medical evaluation, even if the child recovers quickly.

- Keep the umbilical cord stump clean and dry until it falls off (usually 1-3 weeks).
- 2-3 baths a week are enough for young babies. Use lukewarm water and test it with your elbow.
- Gentle massage with a mild oil is fine. Avoid putting oil in the nose or ears.
- Never leave a baby alone in the bath, even for a moment.

- Use a **rear-facing car seat** for as long as the seat allows, and never hold a child on your lap in a moving car.
- Install stair gates, cover sockets, anchor heavy furniture, and keep medicines and chemicals locked away.
- Children can drown in a few centimetres of water, so empty buckets and supervise bath time.

- Feeling tired and overwhelmed is very common, and asking for help is a strength.
- 'Baby blues' usually ease within 2 weeks. If low mood, anxiety or hopelessness lasts longer, please talk to your doctor, since postpartum depression is common and treatable.
- If you ever have thoughts of harming yourself or your baby, seek help immediately: in India you can call **Tele-MANAS at 14416**, or emergency services at 112.
